title: Mathematical Background: Linear Algebra
blurb: Vector spaces, the matrix groups of 3D vision, rank and kernel, eigenvalues, skew-symmetric matrices and the SVD — the toolbox every later chapter is built on, and reliably the largest single problem on the exam (20–28 credits).

knowledge_points.title: Vector Spaces, Span, Linear Independence, Basis
knowledge_points.recap:
**Vector space.** A set $V$ over the field $\mathbb{R}$ that is closed under addition $+:V\times V\to V$ and scalar multiplication $\cdot:\mathbb{R}\times V\to V$, i.e. $\alpha v_1+\beta v_2\in V$ for all $v_i\in V,\ \alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}$. Under $+$ it forms a **commutative (abelian) group** (neutral element $0$, inverse $-v$); scalar multiplication respects $\alpha(\beta u)=(\alpha\beta)u$ and both distributive laws $(\alpha+\beta)v=\alpha v+\beta v$, $\alpha(v+u)=\alpha v+\alpha u$.
**Subspace.** $W\subset V$ with $0\in W$, closed under $+$ and $\cdot$. Note $0\in W$ is what rules out affine sets.
**Span.** $\operatorname{span}(S)=\{v=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\alpha_i v_i\mid v_i\in S,\ \alpha_i\in\mathbb{R}\}$ — the smallest subspace containing $S$.
**Linear independence.** $\sum_{i=1}^{k}\alpha_i v_i=0\ \Rightarrow\ \alpha_i=0\ \forall i$. Equivalently: no vector is a linear combination of the others. The exam MC traps you with the wrong quantifier — it is $\alpha_i=0$, **not** $v_i=0$.
**Basis.** $B=\{v_1,\dots,v_n\}$ that is linearly independent **and** spans $V$; a maximal independent set. Every basis of $V$ has the same number of elements $n=\dim V$, and every $v\in V$ has a **unique** expansion $v=\sum_i\alpha_i b_i$.
**Basis transform.** With $B=(b_1,\dots,b_n)$, $B'=(b'_1,\dots,b'_n)$ as matrices of basis vectors, $B'=BA\iff B=B'A^{-1}$. A linear map $L(x)=Ax$ written in the new basis $P=[e'_1,\dots,e'_n]$ becomes $B=P^{-1}AP$ (same map, new coordinates).
**Useful dimensions.** $\dim\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}=n^2$; symmetric matrices $\dim=\tfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$; skew-symmetric $\dim=\tfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$; $\dim\mathfrak{so}(3)=3$, $\dim\mathfrak{se}(3)=6$.

questions.q: Which of the following sets of vectors is linearly independent?
questions.answer:
Only $\{(4,-5,5)^\top,(-3,1,2)^\top,(2,5,-2)^\top\}$.
**Why the others fail.** For $\{(1,5,9),(8,12,16),(-6,-2,2)\}$ we have $(8,12,16)^\top-2(1,5,9)^\top=(6,2,-2)^\top=-(-6,-2,2)^\top$, so the three are dependent. The set containing the zero vector is always dependent (take $\alpha=1$ on the zero vector). For $\{(2,2,1),(3,1,1),(-1,-7,-2)\}$ one checks $2\,(2,2,1)^\top-\ldots$ gives a non-trivial vanishing combination.
**Fast test.** Three vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$ are independent iff the $3\times3$ determinant is non-zero — but the exam usually wants you to spot the combination by eye.
questions.extend: Zero vector in the set ⇒ dependent, instantly. That is always one of the four options.

questions.q: Let $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k\in\mathbb{R}$. The set of vectors $\{v_1,\dots,v_k\}\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ is called **linearly independent** if …
questions.answer:
$\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_i v_i=0\ \Rightarrow\ \lambda_i=0\ \ \forall i=1,\dots,k$.
**Trap 1.** Concluding $v_i=0$ instead of $\lambda_i=0$ — that would say the vectors themselves vanish.
**Trap 2.** "All vectors are pairwise distinct" is far too weak: $\{v,2v\}$ is distinct but dependent.

questions.q: State the definition of a vector space $V$ over a field $K$. Does $V$ have to satisfy the group properties? What additional properties does a vector space have?
questions.answer:
A vector space $V$ over $K$ satisfies:
**(1)** $(V,+)$ is a **commutative (abelian) group** — so yes, the group axioms are required for addition.
**(2)** A scalar multiplication $\cdot:K\times V\to V$ with $1v=v$, $\alpha(\beta v)=(\alpha\beta)v$, $(\alpha+\beta)v=\alpha v+\beta v$ and $\alpha(v+w)=\alpha v+\alpha w$.
**So:** the additional structure over a plain group is the scalar multiplication together with its compatibility (associativity + two distributive laws) with the field operations.
questions.extend: Scalar multiplication is *not* a group operation — it maps $K\times V\to V$, not $V\times V\to V$.

questions.q: Let $V$ be a vector space over $K$. State the definition of linear independence, of the span of a set $M\subset V$, and of a basis of a subspace $U\subset V$.
questions.answer:
**Linear independence.** $\sum_{i=1}^{k}\alpha_i v_i=0\Rightarrow\alpha_i=0$ for all $i$.
**Span.** $\operatorname{span}(M)=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{k}\alpha_i v_i\ \middle|\ v_i\in M,\ \alpha_i\in K\right\}$.
**Basis.** A linearly independent subset $B\subset U$ with $\operatorname{span}(B)=U$.
questions.extend: Independence answers "is anything redundant?", span answers "do we reach everything?" — a basis needs both.

questions.q: Without using the determinant, decide for $M_1=\left\{(1,1,1)^\top,(0,1,1)^\top,(0,0,1)^\top\right\}$ and $M_2=\left\{(2,1,0)^\top,(1,1,0)^\top\right\}$ whether the set is linearly independent, spans $\mathbb{R}^3$, and forms a basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$.
questions.answer:
**$M_1$.** From $\alpha_1v_1+\alpha_2v_2+\alpha_3v_3=0$ the first component gives $\alpha_1=0$, then the second $\alpha_2=0$, then the third $\alpha_3=0$ — the triangular structure cascades. So $M_1$ is linearly independent. It spans: any $x=(x_1,x_2,x_3)^\top$ is $x_1(v_1-v_2)+(x_2-x_1)v_2+(x_3-x_2)v_3$. Three independent vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$ ⇒ $M_1$ **is a basis**.
**$M_2$.** Independent ($2\alpha_1+\alpha_2=0$ and $\alpha_1+\alpha_2=0$ force $\alpha_1=\alpha_2=0$), but every combination has third component $0$, so it does **not** span $\mathbb{R}^3$ and is **not** a basis.
questions.extend: In $\mathbb{R}^n$: $n$ independent vectors ⇒ automatically a basis; fewer than $n$ ⇒ never a basis.

questions.q: Let $M=[c_1,\dots,c_n]\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$. State the name of the quantity $\dim\big(\operatorname{span}(\{c_1,\dots,c_n\})\big)$.
questions.answer:
The **rank** of the matrix $M$.
**Because** $\operatorname{span}$ of the columns is exactly $\operatorname{range}(M)$, and $\operatorname{rank}(M)=\dim\operatorname{range}(M)$.

questions.q: Let $E=\{A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\mid A^\top=A\}$. What is the dimension of this space?
questions.answer:
$\dim E=\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$.
**Count.** $n$ free diagonal entries plus $\tfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$ free strictly-upper entries (the lower triangle is determined by symmetry).
**Companion fact.** The skew-symmetric matrices form a space of dimension $\tfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$; the two dimensions add to $n^2$ because $\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}=\text{Sym}\oplus\text{Skew}$ with $A=\tfrac12(A+A^\top)+\tfrac12(A-A^\top)$.
questions.extend: $n=3$: symmetric $6$, skew-symmetric $3$ — the $3$ is exactly $\dim\mathfrak{so}(3)$, i.e. the three rotation parameters.

questions.q: Let $L:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n$, $L(x)=Ax$. Let $\{e_i\}$ be the canonical basis and $\{e'_i\}$ another basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$. Define $B=P^{-1}AP$ with $P=[e'_1,\dots,e'_n]$. Describe briefly how $B$ is related to $L$.
questions.answer:
$B$ **represents the same linear map $L$ in the basis $\{e'_i\}$**: it takes the coordinates of $x$ w.r.t. $\{e'_i\}$ and returns the coordinates of $L(x)$ w.r.t. $\{e'_i\}$.
**Read it right to left.** $P$ converts new-basis coordinates to canonical ones, $A$ applies the map, $P^{-1}$ converts back.
**Consequence.** $A$ and $B$ are *similar*, so they share eigenvalues, rank, determinant and trace — $\sigma(B)=\sigma(A)$.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is true for a vector space $(V,+)$ over $\mathbb{R}$?
questions.answer:
**$(V,+)$ with scalar-vector multiplication has to fulfil the distributive law.**
**Why the others fail.** $(V,\cdot)$ is **not** a group — scalar multiplication maps $\mathbb{R}\times V\to V$, not $V\times V\to V$, so it is not even a binary operation on $V$; only $(V,+)$ is a group. Scalar multiplication is a mapping $\mathbb{R}\times V\to V$, **not** $\mathbb{R}\times V\to\mathbb{R}$. And an inner product is **not** part of the definition of a vector space — adding one turns it into an inner-product (Hilbert) space.
questions.extend: Vector space = abelian group under $+$ **plus** a compatible scalar multiplication. Inner product, norm and metric are extra structure.

options.text: The scalar multiplication is defined as a mapping $\mathbb{R}\times V\to\mathbb{R}$.
The $(V,+)$ with scalar-vector multiplication has to fulfil the distributive law.
An inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb{R}$ is defined.

questions.q: Let $B_1=\{\hat e_1,\hat e_2,\hat e_3\}$, where $e_i$ is the $i$-th unit vector in $\mathbb{R}^3$ and $\widehat{\ \cdot\ }$ maps to the skew-symmetric matrix, and let $B_2=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\2\end{pmatrix},\begin{pmatrix}-3\\1\\-6\end{pmatrix},\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}\right\}$. Determine which statement is correct for these sets.
questions.answer:
$\operatorname{span}(B_2)=\left\{(x,y,z)^\top\in\mathbb{R}^3\ \middle|\ x-0.5z=0\right\}$.
**Why.** All three vectors of $B_2$ satisfy $x=\tfrac12z$: $1=\tfrac12\cdot2$ ✓, $-3=\tfrac12(-6)$ ✓, $0=\tfrac12\cdot0$ ✓. So they all lie in that plane and span it (two of them are independent), giving a **2-dimensional** span — hence $B_2$ neither forms a basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$ nor spans it.
**Why $B_1$ fails.** $B_1=\{\hat e_1,\hat e_2,\hat e_3\}$ consists of $3\times3$ **matrices**, not vectors of $\mathbb{R}^3$; it is a basis of $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ (the skew-symmetric matrices), not of $\mathbb{R}^3$ — and certainly not of $SO(3)$, which is a group, not a vector space.
questions.extend: Check whether the candidate vectors satisfy a common linear equation — if they do, they span at most a plane.

questions.q: Which of the following vectors, in addition to the set $B=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\2\end{pmatrix},\begin{pmatrix}-1\\-2\\-1\end{pmatrix},\begin{pmatrix}1\\-3\\1\end{pmatrix}\right\}$, spans $\mathbb{R}^3$?
questions.answer:
$(2,-1,5)^\top$.
**Key observation.** Every vector of $B$ satisfies $x=z$ ($2{=}2$, $-1{=}-1$, $1{=}1$), so all three lie in the plane $\{x=z\}$ and $\operatorname{span}(B)$ is at most **two**-dimensional — $B$ alone does not span $\mathbb{R}^3$, and a set of 4 vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$ certainly *can* span it.
**Test the candidates.** $(2,-1,5)^\top$ has $2\neq5$, so it lies **off** that plane and completes a basis ⇒ the enlarged set spans $\mathbb{R}^3$. $(15,-25,15)^\top$ has $15=15$, so it stays inside the plane and adds nothing.
questions.extend: Find the linear relation the given vectors all satisfy, then pick the candidate that violates it — far quicker than row-reducing a $3\times4$ matrix.

options.text: The given set of vectors spans $\mathbb{R}^3$
A set of 4 vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$ cannot span $\mathbb{R}^3$

knowledge_points.title: Inner Products, Norms and Hilbert Spaces
knowledge_points.recap:
**Inner product.** $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb{R}$ with (1) linearity $\langle u,\alpha v+\beta w\rangle=\alpha\langle u,v\rangle+\beta\langle u,w\rangle$, (2) symmetry $\langle u,v\rangle=\langle v,u\rangle$, (3) positive definiteness $\langle v,v\rangle\ge0$ with equality iff $v=0$.
**Induced norm and metric.** $|v|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ and $d(v,w)=|v-w|$. A finite-dimensional vector space with an inner product is a **Hilbert space**. Orthogonality: $v\perp w\iff\langle v,w\rangle=0$.
**Canonical inner product on $\mathbb{R}^n$.** $\langle x,y\rangle=x^\top y=\sum_i x_iy_i$, inducing the Euclidean $L^2$ norm $|x|_2=\sqrt{x^\top x}$.
**Induced inner product.** After a basis transform $I=B'A^{-1}$, i.e. $x=Ax'$, the canonical product reads $\langle x,y\rangle=x'^\top A^\top A\,y'\equiv\langle x',y'\rangle_{A^\top A}$ — the *induced* inner product of $A$.
**Matrix inner product / Frobenius.** $\langle A,B\rangle=\operatorname{trace}(A^\top B)=\sum_k a_k^\top b_k$, inducing $\|A\|_f=\sqrt{\sum_{ij}a_{ij}^2}=\sqrt{\operatorname{trace}(A^\top A)}=\sqrt{\sigma_1^2+\dots+\sigma_n^2}$. This is the norm used in every projection/Procrustes problem on the exam.
**Induced 2-norm.** $\|A\|_2=\max_{|x|_2=1}|Ax|_2=\sigma_1$ — the largest singular value. $\|A\|_2\neq\|A\|_f$ in general.
**Trace tricks worth memorising.** $\operatorname{trace}(XYZ)=\operatorname{trace}(YZX)=\operatorname{trace}(ZXY)$ (cyclic), $\operatorname{trace}(M)=\operatorname{trace}(M^\top)$, and $\|A\|_f$ is invariant under left/right multiplication by orthogonal matrices.
**Kronecker product and stack.** $A\otimes B$ stacks scaled copies of $B$; $A^s\in\mathbb{R}^{mn}$ stacks the columns of $A$. Key identity: $u^\top A v=(v\otimes u)^\top A^s$ — this is what turns the epipolar constraint into a linear system in Chapter 5.

questions.q: A Hilbert space $H$ is a finite-dimensional vector space over $K$ endowed with an inner product. State the definition of an inner product.
questions.extend: Positive definiteness is only demanded for $v\neq0$ — $\langle 0,0\rangle=0$ is required, not forbidden.

questions.q: Do the following form Hilbert spaces with the given inner product? (a) $\mathbb{R}^n$ with $\langle x,y\rangle=x^\top y$. (b) $\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}$ with $\langle A,B\rangle=\operatorname{trace}(A^\top B)$.
questions.answer:
**(a) Yes.** Symmetry: $x^\top y=\sum_i x_iy_i=y^\top x$. Linearity is immediate. Positive definiteness: $x^\top x=\sum_i x_i^2>0$ for $x\neq0$.
**(b) Yes.** Writing $A=[a_1,\dots,a_m]$ column-wise, $\operatorname{trace}(A^\top B)=\sum_{k=1}^{m}a_k^\top b_k$ — a sum of standard inner products, so all three properties follow from (a).
questions.extend: $\operatorname{trace}(A^\top B)$ is a scalar and needs $A,B$ of identical size. It is *not* $\operatorname{trace}(AB)$.

questions.q: Show that the Frobenius norm $\|A\|_F=\sqrt{\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^2}$ for $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}$ is the norm induced by the inner product $\langle A,B\rangle=\operatorname{trace}(A^\top B)$.
questions.answer:
$\langle A,A\rangle=\operatorname{trace}(A^\top A)=\sum_{k=1}^{m}a_k^\top a_k=\sum_{k=1}^{m}\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{ik}^2=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^2$.
**Hence** $\sqrt{\langle A,A\rangle}=\sqrt{\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^2}=\|A\|_F$, which is exactly the definition of the induced norm $\|A\|=\sqrt{\langle A,A\rangle}$.
questions.extend: Via SVD, $\operatorname{trace}(A^\top A)=\sum_i\sigma_i^2$, so $\|A\|_F=\sqrt{\sigma_1^2+\dots+\sigma_p^2}$ while $\|A\|_2=\sigma_1$.

questions.q: The canonical inner product on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is expressed in a new basis via $x=Ax'$. Which statements about the resulting **induced inner product** are correct?
questions.answer:
$\langle x,y\rangle=x^\top y=(Ax')^\top(Ay')=x'^\top A^\top A\,y'\equiv\langle x',y'\rangle_{A^\top A}$.
**So** the induced product is defined by the symmetric positive (semi-)definite matrix $A^\top A$, and it coincides with the canonical product exactly when $A^\top A=I$, i.e. when $A$ is **orthogonal** — which is precisely why orthogonal transformations preserve lengths and angles.

options.text: The induced product is $\langle x',y'\rangle_{A^\top A}=x'^\top A^\top A\,y'$.
It equals the canonical inner product for every invertible $A$.
It equals the canonical inner product iff $A\in O(n)$.
The matrix $A^\top A$ is symmetric and positive semi-definite.

questions.q: State the Kronecker product and the stack of a matrix, and give the identity that lets a bilinear expression $u^\top A v$ be written as a linear expression in the entries of $A$.
questions.answer:
**Kronecker product.** For $A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$, $B\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times l}$, $A\otimes B=\begin{pmatrix}a_{11}B&\cdots&a_{1n}B\\\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\a_{m1}B&\cdots&a_{mn}B\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{mk\times nl}$.
**Stack.** $A^s=(a_1^\top,\dots,a_n^\top)^\top\in\mathbb{R}^{mn}$, the columns of $A$ stacked on top of each other.
**Identity.** $u^\top A v=(v\otimes u)^\top A^s$.
**Why it matters.** It converts "quadratic in the data, linear in the unknown matrix" into a plain linear system — exactly the step that turns the epipolar constraint $x_2^\top E x_1=0$ into $(x_1\otimes x_2)^\top E^s=0$ for the eight-point algorithm.

questions.q: Using the Frobenius inner product on matrices $A,B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$, defined as $\langle A,B\rangle_F=\operatorname{tr}(A^\top B)$, show that a rotation matrix $R\in SO(n)$ does not change the inner product of two matrices, i.e. $\langle RA,RB\rangle_F=\langle A,B\rangle_F$.
questions.answer:
$$\langle RA,RB\rangle_F=\operatorname{tr}\big((RA)^\top RB\big)=\operatorname{tr}\big(A^\top R^\top RB\big)=\operatorname{tr}\big(A^\top B\big)=\langle A,B\rangle_F,$$
using $R^\top R=I$ for $R\in SO(n)\subset O(n)$.
**Consequence.** Taking $A=B$ gives $\|RA\|_F=\|A\|_F$ — the Frobenius norm is invariant under orthogonal transformations. That invariance is exactly what is used in the orthogonal-Procrustes derivation and in the low-rank approximation error $\|A-A_k\|_F^2=\sum_{i>k}\sigma_i^2$.
questions.extend: The whole proof is "insert $R^\top R=I$". Only orthogonality is needed — $\det R=1$ plays no role here.

knowledge_points.title: Groups and the Matrix Groups of 3D Vision
knowledge_points.recap:
**Group.** A set $G$ with an operation $\circ:G\times G\to G$ satisfying exactly four axioms: **(1) closure** $g_1\circ g_2\in G$; **(2) associativity** $(g_1\circ g_2)\circ g_3=g_1\circ(g_2\circ g_3)$; **(3) neutral element** $\exists e\in G:\ e\circ g=g\circ e=g$; **(4) inverse** $\forall g\ \exists g^{-1}\in G:\ g\circ g^{-1}=g^{-1}\circ g=e$. **Commutativity is *not* an axiom** — that is the single most repeated MC trap.
**$GL(n)$** — general linear group: all $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ with $\det(A)\neq0$.
**$SL(n)$** — special linear group: $\det(A)=1$ (closed because $\det(A^{-1})=\det(A)^{-1}$).
**$O(n)$** — orthogonal group: $R^\top R=RR^\top=I$, equivalently $\langle Rx,Ry\rangle=\langle x,y\rangle$. From $\det(R^\top R)=\det(R)^2=1$ we get $\det(R)\in\{-1,+1\}$.
**$SO(n)=O(n)\cap SL(n)$** — rotations, $\det(R)=+1$ only. $SO(3)$ = all 3D rotation matrices.
**$A(n)$** — affine group: $L(x)=Ax+b$ with $A\in GL(n)$. Not linear unless $b=0$; in homogeneous coordinates it becomes the linear $\begin{pmatrix}A&b\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\in GL(n+1)$.
**$E(n)$** — Euclidean group: $x\mapsto Rx+T$ with $R\in O(n)$. **$SE(n)$** — special Euclidean group, $R\in SO(n)$; $SE(3)$ = the rigid-body motions.
**Inclusions to memorise.** $SO(n)\subset O(n)\subset GL(n)$, $SO(n)\subset SL(n)\subset GL(n)$, and $SE(n)\subset E(n)\subset A(n)\subset GL(n+1)$ — note the $n+1$: the affine/Euclidean groups only become matrix groups after homogenisation. $SL(n)\subset O(n)$ is **false**.
**Standard exam counterexamples.** $\{A\mid\det A=-1\}$ is not a group (no identity, not closed). $\{A\mid\det A>0\}$ *is* a group. Symmetric invertible matrices are not closed under multiplication since $(AB)^\top=BA\neq AB$. $\left\{\begin{pmatrix}A&b\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\right\}$ with $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ **unrestricted** is not a group — invertibility fails unless $A\in GL(n)$.
**Matrix representation.** An injective $R:G\to GL(n)$ with $R(e)=I$ and $R(g\circ h)=R(g)R(h)$ — a group homomorphism, which is why abstract rotations can be studied as matrices.

questions.q: Name the four axioms a group $(G,\circ)$ has to satisfy.
questions.answer:
**(1) Closure:** $g_1\circ g_2\in G$ for all $g_1,g_2\in G$.
**(2) Associativity:** $(g_1\circ g_2)\circ g_3=g_1\circ(g_2\circ g_3)$ for all $g_1,g_2,g_3\in G$.
**(3) Identity / neutral element:** $\exists e\in G$ with $e\circ g=g\circ e=g$ for all $g\in G$.
**(4) Inverse element:** $\forall g\in G\ \exists g^{-1}\in G$ with $g\circ g^{-1}=g^{-1}\circ g=e$.
questions.extend: Strictly, writing the operation as $\circ:M\times M\to M$ already encodes closure — but the exam awards a point for naming it, so always list all four.

questions.q: Which of the following is **not** a necessary condition for a set $G$ with an operation $\circ:G\times G\to G$ to be a group?
questions.answer:
**Commutativity** is not required. A group in which $g_1\circ g_2=g_2\circ g_1$ holds is called *abelian*, which is a strictly stronger notion.
**Counterexample.** $SO(3)$ is a group but rotations do not commute — $R_xR_y\neq R_yR_x$ in general.
questions.extend: Matrix multiplication is associative but not commutative — every matrix group is a live counterexample.

options.text: Associativity: $(g_1\circ g_2)\circ g_3=g_1\circ(g_2\circ g_3)\ \forall g_1,g_2,g_3\in G$
Neutral element: $\exists e\in G:\ e\circ g=g\circ e=g\ \forall g\in G$

questions.q: Consider the set $G$ of all matrices of the form $\begin{pmatrix}A&b\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, where $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$, $b\in\mathbb{R}^n$, and let $\circ$ be matrix multiplication. Is $(G,\circ)$ a group? If so, give the name of this group; if not, explain why.
questions.answer:
**It is not a group.**
**Reason.** The elements of $G$ are not invertible whenever the top-left block $A$ is singular — nothing in the definition forces $\det(A)\neq0$, so the inverse axiom fails.
**Fix.** Restricting to $A\in GL(n)$ *does* give a group: the **affine group $A(n)$**, a subgroup of $GL(n+1)$, with $\begin{pmatrix}A&b\\0&1\end{pmatrix}^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}A^{-1}&-A^{-1}b\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$.
questions.extend: Read the constraint on $A$ very carefully: $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ ⇒ no group; $A\in GL(n)$ ⇒ affine group $A(n)$.

questions.q: Let $A\in GL(n)$, $b\in\mathbb{R}^n$, $c\in\mathbb{R}^n$ with $c=0$. Consider the group of all matrices $\begin{pmatrix}A&b\\c^\top&1\end{pmatrix}$ under matrix multiplication. State the name of this group.
questions.answer:
The **affine group $A(n)$**.
**Why.** With $c=0$ the matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}A&b\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, the homogeneous-coordinate representation of $x\mapsto Ax+b$. Because $A$ is required to be invertible here, closure and inverses hold, and $A(n)$ is a subgroup of $GL(n+1)$.

questions.q: Which of the following sets represents all the possible values of determinants of a matrix in $SO(n)$?
questions.answer:
$\{1\}$.
**Derivation.** $SO(n)=O(n)\cap SL(n)$, so orthogonality forces $\det(R)^2=1\Rightarrow\det(R)=\pm1$, and the *special* condition then keeps only $\det(R)=+1$.
**Contrast with $O(n)$,** whose determinants are $\{-1,+1\}$ — the $-1$ elements are the reflections.

questions.q: Which of the following sets represents all the possible values of determinants of a matrix in $O(n)$?
questions.answer:
$\{-1,+1\}$.
**Derivation.** $R^\top R=I\Rightarrow\det(R^\top R)=\det(R)^2=\det(I)=1$, hence $\det(R)=\pm1$. Both values occur: $I$ has determinant $+1$, any reflection has $-1$.

questions.q: Show that the set $O(n)=\{R\in GL(n)\mid R^\top R=I\}$ is **closed** under matrix multiplication.
questions.answer:
Let $A,B\in O(n)$. Then
$$(AB)^\top AB=B^\top A^\top A B=B^\top I B=B^\top B=I,$$
using $A^\top A=I$ and $B^\top B=I$. Hence $AB\in O(n)$, so $O(n)$ is closed under matrix multiplication.
questions.extend: The whole proof is "insert $A^\top A=I$, then $B^\top B=I$" — write both steps, they are worth a point each.

questions.q: Show that the set $O(n)$ is **associative** with matrix multiplication.
questions.answer: Matrix multiplication is associative for all matrices, and $O(n)$ is closed under matrix multiplication (previous part), so every product of elements of $O(n)$ stays inside $O(n)$ and inherits associativity: $(AB)C=A(BC)$ for all $A,B,C\in O(n)$.
questions.extend: Associativity is never proved from scratch — you cite the ambient operation plus closure. Mentioning closure is what earns the second point.

questions.q: Show that the set $O(n)$ contains the neutral element (the identity matrix) with matrix multiplication.
questions.answer: $I^\top I=II=I$, since $I^\top=I$ and $I\cdot I=I$. Hence $I\in O(n)$, and $IA=AI=A$ for every $A\in O(n)$, so $I$ is the neutral element.

questions.q: Show that the set $O(n)$ contains an inverse element for each of its elements.
questions.answer:
Each $R\in O(n)$ has $\det(R)=\pm1\neq0$, so $R^{-1}$ exists.
**Identify it.** From $R^\top R=I$, multiplying on the right by $R^{-1}$ gives $R^\top=R^{-1}$.
**Show it stays in $O(n)$.** $(R^{-1})^\top R^{-1}=(R^\top)^\top R^{-1}=RR^{-1}=I$, so $R^{-1}=R^\top\in O(n)$.
questions.extend: For orthogonal matrices, transpose = inverse. This single fact drives $g^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}R^\top&-R^\top T\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ in Chapter 2.

questions.q: In the lecture you have seen the groups $O(n)$, $A(n)$, $E(n)$, $SE(n)$, $SO(n)$ and $GL(n)$ with $n\in\mathbb{N}$. Which subset relations are true?
questions.answer:
True: $SE(n)\subset A(n)$, $SO(n)\subset GL(n)$, $SE(n)\subset GL(n+1)$.
**False:** $O(n)\subset SO(n)$ (the inclusion runs the other way — $SO(n)$ is the subgroup with $\det=+1$); $A(n)\subset E(n)$ (again reversed: Euclidean transformations are the affine ones with orthogonal $A$); $SE(n)\subset GL(n)$ — rigid motions are $(n+1)\times(n+1)$ homogeneous matrices, so they embed in $GL(n+1)$, **not** $GL(n)$.
**Chain to remember:** $SE(n)\subset E(n)\subset A(n)\subset GL(n+1)$.
questions.extend: Whenever $A(n)$, $E(n)$ or $SE(n)$ meets $GL$, the answer carries $n+1$.

questions.q: Tick the correct statement.
questions.answer:
$SE(n)\subset A(n)\subset GL(n+1)$.
**Why the $n+1$.** An affine map $x\mapsto Ax+b$ is only linear after homogenisation, where it becomes the $(n+1)\times(n+1)$ matrix $\begin{pmatrix}A&b\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ — an element of $GL(n+1)$, not of $GL(n)$.
**And** $GL$ is never contained in $O$: orthogonality is a restriction, so $O(n)\subset GL(n)$.

questions.q: Tick the **wrong** statement.
questions.answer:
$SL(n)\subset O(n)$ is wrong.
**Counterexample.** $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ has determinant $1$, so it lies in $SL(2)$, but it is not orthogonal.
**Correct relation.** It goes the other way round only for the *special* orthogonal part: $SO(n)=O(n)\cap SL(n)\subset SL(n)$. The other three statements — $E(n)\subset A(n)$, $SO(n)\subset O(n)$, $SE(n)\subset GL(n+1)$ — are all true.

questions.q: Let $(M,\cdot)$ be a group with right identity $e\in M$ ($a\cdot e=a$) and right inverse $a^{-1}\in M$ ($a\cdot a^{-1}=e$). Show that the right identity is also a left identity and the right inverse is also a left inverse.
questions.answer:
**Left inverse first.** Set $b=a^{-1}$; $b$ has its own right inverse $b^{-1}$ with $b\cdot b^{-1}=e$. Then
$$b\cdot a=(b\cdot a)\cdot e=(b\cdot a)(b\cdot b^{-1})=b\,(a\cdot b)\,b^{-1}=b\,(a\cdot a^{-1})\,b^{-1}=b\cdot e\cdot b^{-1}=b\cdot b^{-1}=e,$$
so $a^{-1}\cdot a=e$.
**Then left identity.** $e\cdot a=(a\cdot a^{-1})\cdot a=a\cdot(a^{-1}\cdot a)=a\cdot e=a$.
questions.extend: Order matters: prove the left inverse first, then reuse it for the left identity. You may only use associativity plus the two right-sided assumptions.

questions.q: Let $(M,\cdot)$ be a group. Show that the inverse element $a^{-1}$ of $a\in M$ is unique.
questions.answer:
Suppose $c\in M$ also satisfies $a\cdot c=e$. Then
$$c=e\cdot c=(a^{-1}\cdot a)\cdot c=a^{-1}\cdot(a\cdot c)=a^{-1}\cdot e=a^{-1}.$$
So any element behaving as an inverse equals $a^{-1}$ — the inverse is unique.
questions.extend: Standard uniqueness pattern: assume a second candidate, then derive that it equals the first.

questions.q: Which of the following sets forms a group under matrix multiplication? Prove or disprove. (a) $G_1=\{A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\mid\det(A)\neq0,\ A^\top=A\}$ (b) $G_2=\{A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\mid\det(A)=-1\}$ (c) $G_3=\{A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\mid\det(A)>0\}$
questions.answer:
**(a) Not a group.** Closure fails: for $A,B\in G_1$, $(AB)^	op=B^	op A^	op=BA
eq AB$ in general, so the product need not be symmetric.
**(b) Not a group.** No identity: $\det(I)=1
eq-1$. Closure also fails, since $\det(AB)=(-1)(-1)=1
otin G_2$.
**(c) Yes, a group** (a subgroup of $GL(n)$). Identity: $\det(I)=1>0$. Closure: $\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B)>0$. Inverse: $\det(A^{-1})=1/\det(A)>0$. Associativity is inherited from matrix multiplication.
questions.extend: Check the identity first — it is the cheapest axiom to falsify, and it kills every "$\det=c$" set with $c\neq1$.

questions.q: Which groups were mentioned in the lecture? Write down the names and the correct inclusions.
questions.answer:
**Groups.** $GL(n)$ general linear, $SL(n)$ special linear, $O(n)$ orthogonal, $SO(n)$ special orthogonal, $A(n)$ affine, $E(n)$ Euclidean, $SE(n)$ special Euclidean.
**Inclusions.** $SO(n)\subset O(n)\subset GL(n)$; $SO(n)\subset SL(n)\subset GL(n)$; $SE(n)\subset E(n)\subset A(n)\subset GL(n+1)$.
**Note.** $A(n)$, $E(n)$, $SE(n)$ are $(n+1)\times(n+1)$ matrices in homogeneous coordinates, hence the $GL(n+1)$.
questions.extend: $SO(n)$ sits in *both* $O(n)$ and $SL(n)$ — in fact $SO(n)=O(n)\cap SL(n)$.

questions.q: Determine which statement is correct.
questions.answer:
**$\operatorname{sym}(3)=\{A\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times3}\mid A=A^\top\}$ is a subvectorspace of $\mathbb{R}^{3\times3}$ over $\mathbb{R}$ with matrix addition.**
**Why.** The symmetric matrices contain $0$ and are closed under addition and scalar multiplication ($(\alpha A+\beta B)^\top=\alpha A+\beta B$), so they form a linear subspace — of dimension $\tfrac{n(n+1)}{2}=6$.
**Why the $SO(3)$ options fail.** $SO(3)$ **is** a group under matrix multiplication, but it is a subgroup of $GL(3)$, not of $\mathbb{R}^{3\times3}$ (which is not a group under multiplication — singular matrices have no inverse), and certainly not of $\mathbb{R}^3$. It is **not** a vector space at all: $0\notin SO(3)$ and the sum of two rotations is generally not a rotation.
questions.extend: $SO(3)$ is a curved manifold and a group; $\operatorname{sym}(n)$ and $\mathfrak{so}(n)$ are flat vector spaces. Do not mix the two structures.

options.text: $SO(3)$ is a subgroup of $\mathbb{R}^{3\times3}$ with the matrix multiplication.
$SO(3)$ is a vectorspace over $\mathbb{R}$ with the matrix addition.
$SO(3)$ is a subvectorspace of $\mathbb{R}^{3\times3}$ vectorspace over $\mathbb{R}$ with the matrix addition.
$\operatorname{sym}(3)=\{A\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times3}\mid A=A^\top\}$ is a subvectorspace of $\mathbb{R}^{3\times3}$ over $\mathbb{R}$ with the matrix addition.
$SO(3)$ is a subgroup of $\mathbb{R}^3$ with the matrix multiplication.

questions.answer:
**Incorrect:** "In general, for a matrix $B\in SE(n)$, $\det(B)
eq1$."
**Why.** An element of $SE(n)$ is $ egin{pmatrix}R&T\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ with $R\in SO(n)$, so its determinant is $\det(R)\cdot1=1$ — **always** exactly $1$, never anything else.
**The others are correct.** A general $B\in GL(n+1)$ only needs $\det(B)
eq0$, so in general $\det(B)

questions.extend: $\det=1$ is exactly what the "special" in special Euclidean / special orthogonal / special linear means.
